title: Grace to a broken women part 4
scripture_text: ‘’Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he appeared again in the temple courts, where all the people gathered around him, and he sat down to teach them. The teachers of the law and the Pharisees brought in a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before the group and said to Jesus, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. In the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?” They were using this question as a trap, in order to have a basis for accusing him. But Jesus bent down and started to write on the ground with his finger. When they kept on questioning him, he straightened up and said to them, “Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground. At this, those who heard began to go away one at a time, the older ones first, until only Jesus was left, with the woman still standing there. Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” “No one, sir,” she said. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Go now and leave your life of sin.”
devotional:
The response of Jesus

As the sun rises over the temple precincts, Jesus is faced with a theological and moral dilemma and everyone present waits to see how we responds. As we stand with the crowds, let us watch intently and listen carefully as Jesus demonstrate the transforming power of grace…

There are a few things worth noting here about Jesus’ response:

He didn’t speak. ‘But Jesus stooped down and wrote in the dust with his finger.’ This was totally unexpected. The Teachers of the Law and the Pharisees were probably expecting some kind of verbal response from Jesus, so his silence must have infuriated them. They are feeling ignored and we read that they ‘demanded an answer’. But Jesus slows everything down. He dictates the pace. He takes the situation out of the hands of the Pharisees and takes it into his own hands.

Try and imagine the tension at this point. The Pharisees feel they have caught Jesus in a trap, and they are longing for him to incriminate himself, but he says nothing.

Sometimes in tense situations we can say more without the use of words.

There has been much debate about what Jesus may have written, but John doesn’t tell us, so it mustn’t be important for us to know. However, Jesus writing on the ground must have taken the focus away from the woman.

When Jesus finally stands and speaks, he says ‘If any of you are without sin let him be the first to throw a stone at her.’

Notice Jesus doesn’t speak about the woman, but rather about the heart attitude of the self-righteous Pharisees. Jesus was exposing their sin; he was refusing to let them hide behind the sin of the woman. What he says, in effect, is, "You are no better off than she is. Your hearts are filled with murder and hatred."

Jesus allows them to leave without saying anything more to them. ‘At this, those who heard began to go away one at a time, the oldest ones first, until only Jesus was left with the woman standing there.”

With a simple word Jesus has diffused the tension and one by one, the stones are dropped and the Pharisees leave. It may be that the older ones realized that their trap for Jesus didn’t work, and according to Roman law they had no powers of execution. Or perhaps they had more sin in their hearts. Either way, the accusers gradually leave the scene, leaving Jesus to deal with the woman.

Jesus and the woman.

“until only Jesus was left with the woman standing there.”

I think this is one of the most beautiful and holiest moments in the bible. All the accusers have gone, and probably the crowds with them, and a frail, fragile guilt-filled woman lies on the ground before the Lord Jesus. Her heart is pounding, her mouth is dry, her palms are sweaty…what will he say?

He doesn’t question her; he doesn’t investigate to see if she might be innocent – they both know she is guilty. But in tender mercy he says,

‘Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you.’ ‘No one Sir, she said. ‘Then neither do I condemn you,’ Jesus said, ‘Go and sin no more.’

Notice the order of what Jesus says: "Neither do I condemn you. Go and sin no more."

First God assures us of his forgiveness; then he calls on us to cooperate with him as he liberates us from a life of sin.

Why is this order so important?

Because of the way God motivates us to live for him.

RELIGION SAYS: "Change, or I will condemn you." The fear and threat of God's condemnation is always potentially hanging over our heads in order to "keep us in line." This will not promote deep and lasting change. People who live under by this principle tend to have a superficial and self-righteous kind of holiness.

By contrast, GRACE SAYS: "I have forgiven and accepted you. Now respond to my love by allowing me to change your life.

Loving gratitude is the most powerful motivator in the universe. We don't change in order to be accepted, but because we have been accepted. Real righteousness is practising love toward God and others. Nothing motivates this kind of lifestyle like forgiveness received. This is why grace, properly understood and appropriated, produces a superior righteousness in the lifestyle of its recipient.

That is what’s so amazing about grace!

Grace isn’t fair…but it is right. Grace is always appropriate, no matter what the context.

You could read this story and simply think that Jesus is soft on sinners – a bit like an indulgent parent who continues to let their child ‘off the hook’ – as long as they promise to be a good girl or boy and not do it again.

How do we reconcile the grace of God with the widespread damage and hurt caused by adultery or other sin that destroys people and relationships. How can Jesus forgive so freely? Is he just like an indulgent parent who lets things go unchecked and doesn’t deal with the heart of the matter?

Maybe this is one of the reasons why we struggle so much with grace, it seems to undermine justice and fairness. To think that God loves the person who has caused you so much pain and distress, just as much as he loves you, can be an unsettling thought. Grace understands and accepts that no matter how guilty a person may be, their misdeeds, or mistreatment of us cannot reduce their value as people who are still loved by God, and people whom God wants us to love too, and that is very difficult.

You could say that this story of the lady caught in adultery contains one of the greatest ‘miracles’ of Jesus’ ministry. A lady, whose life was shaped and marked with guilt and shame, was set free to go and sin no more. This is the power of grace.
prayer: Father thank you for the beauty of the grace that Jesus gives us.
